chapters.chapter_text: Mrs. Perera placed a small 1000 µF capacitor on the desk and smiled. “This little part is a capacitor,” she said. “It can store static electric charges.” Nimal connected it carefully to three dry cells with pieces of wire, making sure the terminals were joined correctly. They waited for a few seconds, and Anjali watched the capacitor as if it were a tiny battery holding a secret. When Mrs. Perera removed the dry cells and connected a small LED to the capacitor, the LED glowed for a moment. “That glow happens because the capacitor is discharging,” she explained. “The stored charges are released through the LED.” Nimal leaned closer, and the teacher reminded him that the positive terminal must be connected to the positive side of the LED. The children repeated the activity and saw that the capacitor could be charged again and again. On the board, Mrs. Perera wrote two important words: charging and discharging. “Charging means storing electric charges in the capacitor,” she said, “and discharging means releasing them.” She also showed them the symbol used for a capacitor and pointed out that capacitors come in different sizes. “The amount of charge a capacitor can store is measured in Farads, and microfarad, written µF, is a smaller unit,” she added. Before the bell rang, Anjali looked at the little component with new respect. It was not just a part in a circuit; it was a clever charge keeper. Mrs. Perera told the class that capacitors are found in many electronic devices, and that next time they would look at where such parts appear in radios, televisions, and CFLs.

chapters.chapter_text: After lunch, Mrs. Perera brought a small box to the science club table. "Today we are meeting a special part called a capacitor," she said. Nimal watched as she showed a simple circuit with a battery, a bulb, and a tiny capacitor. "A capacitor stores electric charge for a short time, like a tiny energy keeper," she explained. The friends leaned closer when the bulb blinked on and off as the capacitor charged and discharged. Dilani asked why it was not like a battery. Mrs. Perera smiled. "A battery makes electrical energy from chemicals for a longer time, but a capacitor stores charge and releases it quickly." She drew two metal plates with a gap between them. "Inside, the plates collect opposite charges. That stored charge can later flow out and help in things like camera flashes and some electronic timers." Farhan nodded, imagining a flash of light in a split second. To make it real, Mrs. Perera charged a capacitor in the circuit and then disconnected the battery. The bulb still glowed for a short moment, and Sana gasped. "See?" said Mrs. Perera. "The capacitor had saved some electric energy and gave it back little by little." The friends wrote in their notebooks that a capacitor does not create electricity; it stores electrical energy in an electric field between its plates. Before the bell rang, Mrs. Perera pointed to the school gate alarm board. "We will use capacitors again when we learn about timing circuits," she said. Nimal looked at the tiny part with new respect. It was small, but it could hold charge, release energy, and help machines work at the right moment.

chapters.chapter_text: On a warm June morning in Weligama, Anjali looked at the sky before school and said, “It feels different today.” Ms. Perera smiled and explained that weather means the short-term condition of the atmosphere, such as temperature, rainfall, humidity, and wind. She pointed to the class table and showed how students record daily weather instead of guessing it from one feeling alone. Kasun read the figures for Colombo from the textbook chart and was surprised. On some days the maximum temperature was the same, and on other days the minimum temperature was the same. Ms. Perera explained that a thermometer measures temperature, and a rain gauge measures rainfall. The class also learned that the day with the highest rainfall was 22.35 mm, so weather can change from one day to the next even in the same month. Then the teacher asked the children to look outside the classroom window. The coconut leaves bent gently, and Anjali said the wind seemed stronger than in the morning. Ms. Perera said that people can also observe wind direction and speed, and that a wind vane and an anemometer are used for this. She reminded them that humidity means the amount of water vapour in the air, which is why some days feel sticky and heavy. By the end of the lesson, the children began their booklet about how people observe weather. Kasun wrote that weather is not the same as climate, because weather changes day by day while climate describes a place over a longer time. Anjali drew a rain gauge beside a bright sun, ready to continue the story of Weligama’s sky tomorrow.

chapters.chapter_text: One morning, Aaloka and Nethmi noticed that the sky over the hills looked pale and hazy instead of bright blue. Granny pointed to the swaying jak tree and said, “Today the weather may change.” Aaloka remembered that weather means the condition of the air at a certain time and place, like sunshine, clouds, wind, or rain. By midday, the warm sun had dried the yard, and little wisps of water seemed to disappear from the puddles near the tap. Granny explained that the water was evaporating, turning from liquid into invisible water vapour and rising into the air. “When that vapour cools high up, it can form clouds,” she said, while Nethmi watched a fat cloud grow bigger over the village. Soon a cool breeze moved across the paddy field, and the clouds became darker. Aaloka felt tiny drops on his nose, then a soft rain began to fall on the roof. He laughed and held out his hand. “Weather can change very quickly,” Granny said. “That is why farmers and schoolchildren in Sri Lanka always watch the sky carefully.”

chapters.chapter_text: Nethu placed a compass on the bench and watched the needle settle quietly. “It always turns the same way,” she said. Ms. Perera smiled and explained that when a compass is free from other magnets, its north pole points in one direction because Earth itself has a large magnetic field around it. This is called geomagnetism, and the compass needle lines up with that field. Amal held a bar magnet near the compass, and the needle turned at once. “So the compass shows magnetic field direction,” he said. Ms. Perera nodded and added that the direction shown by the compass is called magnetic north. It is not exactly the same as real north; it lies a little to the north-west of it. The students then noticed that no matter how they turned the compass on the table, its needle kept aligning along the same north-south direction. Ms. Perera explained that free magnets and compasses behave this way because Earth’s magnetic field reaches all around us. “That is why sailors and travelers once used compasses to find direction,” she said, tapping the map on the wall. Before the bell rang, Ms. Perera told them one more thing: magnets can lose power if they are exposed to high temperature, strong vibrations, or strong magnetic fields. Nethu carefully placed the compass back in the box and smiled. She had learned that even the Earth is like a giant invisible magnet guiding tiny needles across the classroom.

chapters.chapter_text: On a bright Friday afternoon, Nuwan and Ayesha hurried to the school science room, where Ms. Perera had placed a small compass, a bar magnet, and a map of Sri Lanka on the table. “Today,” she said, smiling, “we are learning about geomagnetism—the Earth’s magnetic field.” Ayesha turned the compass slowly, and the needle always settled in one direction. “It is not pointing to a random place,” Ms. Perera explained. “The Earth itself behaves like a giant magnet.” Ms. Perera drew a simple sketch of the Earth and its magnetic field lines. She explained that these invisible lines spread out around our planet and help compass needles point north and south. Nuwan asked, “So the compass is actually feeling the Earth’s magnetism?” “Exactly,” she said. “The needle is a tiny magnet, and it lines up with Earth’s magnetic field.” The children looked at the compass again, now imagining the whole planet around them as a giant invisible magnet. Then Ms. Perera held the bar magnet near the compass. The needle jumped and turned. “This shows that magnets can affect other magnets,” she said. “But Earth’s magnetic field is much bigger, and it protects us too. It helps block some harmful particles from the Sun.” Ayesha remembered hearing about the Sun’s strong energy and was surprised that an invisible force around Earth could help guard life. Before the club ended, Ms. Perera pointed to the map of Sri Lanka and said, “A compass works because of geomagnetism, but remember, magnetic north is not exactly the same as geographic north on a map.” Nuwan nodded carefully, thinking that science was full of hidden directions. As they packed their books, the compass lay quietly on the table, still pointing north, as if the Earth itself was whispering the way forward.

chapters.chapter_text: On a rainy afternoon, the Grade 7 science club crowded around the sink in the lab. Ms. Perera held a small turbine made with metal blades fixed to a cork stopper and said, “Let’s see what moving water can do.” When she opened the tap, the water rushed down and the blades spun fast. Kasun laughed, “The water is doing work!” Ms. Perera nodded and explained that moving objects have energy, and the energy in a moving object is called kinetic energy. Nadeesha then pushed a toy car toward a small ball on the table. The ball rolled away after the car hit it, and everyone noticed that work had been done again. “So the moving car had kinetic energy too,” Nadeesha said. Ms. Perera added that flowing water, a moving vehicle, and even a moving pebble are examples of things with kinetic energy. The class wrote down their observations carefully, because this was the first clue that motion itself can carry energy. Next, Ms. Perera pointed to the turbine and asked, “Can we use this moving water to make electricity?” She explained that when energy changes from one form to another, it is called energy transformation. In a windmill, the kinetic energy of wind can be changed into electrical energy by a dynamo; in a hydropower station, the kinetic energy of water is also used to generate electricity. The children imagined the river outside school turning a turbine and lighting up homes far away. Before the bell rang, Ms. Perera smiled and said, “A river at a higher place can flow down and do work, but today we focused on the energy in the moving water itself.” The class left the lab excited, with one more question in their minds: if wind and water can turn motion into useful electricity, what other moving things around them might be hiding kinetic energy?

chapters.chapter_text: On a bright afternoon, Nisha carried a plastic bottle filled with marbles to the school science club. Ms. Perera asked the class to place the bottle at the top of the small grassy slope near the playground. When Kasun gave it a gentle push, the bottle rolled faster and faster downhill, making the marbles rattle like tiny drums. "That moving bottle has kinetic energy," Ms. Perera said. "Kinetic energy is the energy an object has because it is moving." She explained that the faster the bottle moved, the more kinetic energy it had. Nisha noticed that the bottle at the bottom looked as if it wanted to keep going, and Ms. Perera nodded. "An object with more mass and more speed can have more kinetic energy." Then the teacher placed two balls on the ground: a light rubber ball and a heavier cricket ball. She rolled both balls at the same speed and asked which one would have more kinetic energy. Kasun guessed the cricket ball, because it was heavier, and he was right. The class also saw that when the bottle finally stopped, its kinetic energy had changed into sound, a little heat, and motion in the marbles. As the bell rang, Nisha smiled. She realized that every moving thing around her—an open door swinging in the wind, a running child, even a spinning top—can carry kinetic energy. Next time, she thought, she would watch the school cricket match with new eyes. When the bottle finally stopped, what happened to its kinetic energy? It disappeared completely without changing form. It changed into sound, heat, and motion in the marbles. It turned into light only. It became chemical energy inside the bottle.

chapters.chapter_text: Aruni looked at the glowing bulb on the desk and asked, “Sir, why does the bulb get dimmer when we add another part to the circuit?” Mr. Perera smiled and placed a small metal piece beside the wires. “That piece is a resistor,” he said. “The obstacle a conductor gives to the flow of electric current is called resistance. We use the symbol R for resistance, and its unit is the ohm, written as Ω.” Nimal connected the resistor into the circuit, and the ammeter reading became smaller. “So the current has decreased,” he said. Mr. Perera nodded. “Yes. When resistance increases, current decreases. That is why resistors are useful: they help us control the current in a circuit.” He showed them a box of fixed resistors and explained that components made with different resistance values can be added to circuits for this purpose. Then he pointed to the connecting wires. “Copper wires are used for connections because their resistance is very low,” he said. “But metals like nichrome have much higher resistance, so they are used to make resistors. The value of a resistor is often shown by a colour code on it.” Aruni carefully copied the colour bands in her notebook, feeling as if the tiny stripes were secret messages from the wire itself. Before the bell rang, Mr. Perera added, “Remember, current can be controlled by changing resistance.” The students packed up their circuit materials, excited to test more resistors in the next lesson. Outside, the Kandy afternoon was bright, but inside the science room, the little idea of resistance had made the current story even brighter. When the bell rang, Mr. Perera reminded them that the flow of current in a circuit can be adjusted, just like turning a tap. The class left wondering which resistor would make the bulb glow just right in their next experiment.

chapters.chapter_text: On a rainy afternoon at St. Anne’s College in Kandy, Nadeesha and Imran were trying to fix a small torch for the science club display. The bulb would glow brightly when they used a short wire, but when they replaced it with a much longer wire, the bulb became dim. Mrs. Perera smiled and said, “That is because the wire’s resistance has changed.” She explained that resistance is the opposition a conductor gives to the flow of electric current. In simple words, it is like the wire’s “difficulty” for electricity to pass through. A longer wire has more resistance because the electrons must travel a bigger distance and meet more obstacles on the way, while a thicker wire usually has less resistance because there is more space for the current to move. Nadeesha compared it to walking through a narrow corridor versus a wide hall, and the class laughed. Mrs. Perera nodded and added that resistance depends on the length, thickness, and material of the conductor. Copper wire is often used in homes because it has low resistance, so it allows current to flow easily. By the end of the period, the torch glowed steadily again, and Imran wrote the important rule in his notebook: longer wire, more resistance; thicker wire, less resistance. Nadeesha tucked the wire into the box and wondered what other school gadgets they could repair using this new idea.

chapters.chapter_text: On a rainy afternoon, Ms. Perera placed a red-and-blue cardboard shape on the table. “Today we will build the human heart,” she said. Nethu looked at the model and noticed it was divided into four chambers: two upper atria and two lower ventricles. “The right atrium and left atrium are on top, and the right ventricle and left ventricle are below,” Ms. Perera explained, drawing the names carefully on the board. Malith pointed to two flaps made from black paper. “Those are the valves,” he guessed. Ms. Perera nodded. “Yes. The bicuspid valve lies between the left atrium and left ventricle, and the tricuspid valve lies between the right atrium and right ventricle. These valves help blood move in the correct direction.” Nethu smiled as the model began to make sense, like a tiny house with doors that open the right way. Then Ms. Perera added two thick tubes to the bottom of the model. “These are the main arteries connected to the ventricles. The aorta starts from the left ventricle, and the pulmonary artery starts from the right ventricle. At the start of each one is a semilunar valve.” She also fixed two thinner tubes at the top. “The superior vena cava and inferior vena cava open into the right atrium, while the left and right pulmonary veins open into the left atrium.” By the time the bell rang, the paper heart stood proudly on the desk. Nethu looked at it one last time and whispered, “So the heart is not just one pump—it has chambers, valves, arteries, and veins all arranged neatly.” Ms. Perera smiled. “Exactly. And next time, we will follow how blood moves through this wonderful organ.”

chapters.chapter_text: On a rainy afternoon at Galle Central College, Ms. Perera placed a clay model on the lab table and smiled. “Today,” she said, “we are visiting the human heart.” Nimal leaned closer as Ishani lifted the model’s top half. Inside, they saw that the heart was not one single empty room but a strong muscular organ divided into four chambers: two upper atria and two lower ventricles. “The atria receive blood,” Ms. Perera explained, “and the ventricles pump it out with force.” Ishani pointed to a thick wall running down the middle of the model. “Why is the heart split like that?” she asked. “That wall is the septum,” said Ms. Perera. “It keeps oxygen-rich blood and oxygen-poor blood separate.” She then showed them the right side and left side of the heart. “The right side sends blood to the lungs to get oxygen, while the left side sends oxygen-rich blood to the rest of the body.” Nimal nodded, imagining the heart as a busy double station. Ms. Perera traced the tiny tube-like openings on the model. “These are blood vessels connected to the heart. The heart has arteries that carry blood away, and veins that bring blood back. The valves act like doors, opening one way only, so blood does not flow backward.” Ishani laughed softly. “So the heart is like a pump with doors and separate rooms!” “Exactly,” said Ms. Perera. “And that smart structure helps it keep blood moving every second of our lives.” As the rain tapped the classroom window, Nimal placed his hand on his chest and felt his own steady beat. The heart seemed small for such an important job, but its chambers, septum, and valves worked together like a carefully planned machine. He knew that in the next lesson, they would discover how this powerful pump actually keeps beating day and night without stopping.

chapters.chapter_text: Nethu bent down near a shoe flower bush and smiled. "Ayyo, these plants all look different!" she said, noticing a small herb, a tall tree, and a bright flower beside the garden path. Mrs. Perera told the class that flowering plants show great diversity in size and morphological features, but they all have some common main parts: roots, stem, leaves, flowers, fruits, and seeds. The teacher gently pointed to a small plant and said, "This is the root system below the soil, and above it is the shoot system." Nethu traced the stem with her finger, then found the leaves, flowers, and tiny fruits on another plant. "So the plant body has parts we can observe and compare," Amal said, as they wrote the names in their field book. At the shoe flower, Mrs. Perera opened a half flower and showed them the sepals, petals, androecium, and gynoecium. "Sepals are usually green and protect the flower bud," she explained. "Petals are bright and help attract insects for pollination. The androecium is the male part and makes pollen, while the gynoecium is the female part and helps produce seeds." Nethu looked carefully at the stigma, style, ovary, and ovules, feeling as if the flower had hidden secrets. Before the bell rang, Mrs. Perera added, "Flowers make fruits, and the seeds inside fruits grow into new plants." She also pointed to two other plants in the garden and asked the children to notice a simple difference: one had leaves with parallel venation and three-petal-like flowers, while another had leaves with reticulate venation and flowers with four or five petals. Nethu laughed softly. "Now the garden feels like a science lesson in pieces!"

chapters.chapter_text: After school, Nimali, Sahan, and Ruwan followed their science teacher, Ms. Perera, into the school garden. She stopped beside a bright red hibiscus plant and said, “Today we are learning the morphological features of flowering plants—the outside parts we can see and use to identify a plant.” The children looked carefully at the plant’s roots, stem, leaves, and flowers. Ms. Perera explained that the roots held the plant in the soil and absorbed water and minerals, while the stem supported the plant and carried water upward. Nimali gently touched a leaf. “Why does it have a broad shape?” she asked. Ms. Perera smiled and said broad leaves can catch more sunlight for making food. She pointed to the leaf stalk, called the petiole, and the leaf blade, called the lamina. “Look closely at the veins too,” she said. “They help transport materials and give support to the leaf.” Ruwan noticed that some leaves grew one by one along the stem, which Ms. Perera called an alternate arrangement. Then they examined the flower. The hibiscus had five colorful petals, green sepals at the base, and a long tube in the center. “Flowers are the reproductive part of the plant,” Ms. Perera explained. “The sepals protect the bud, and the petals attract insects for pollination.” She pointed out the stamen, the male part, and the pistil, the female part. The children were surprised that such a beautiful flower was also a tiny seed-making factory. Before leaving, Ms. Perera asked them to compare the hibiscus with a nearby grass plant. “Not all flowering plants look the same,” she said. “Some have tap roots, some have fibrous roots, and leaves may have different shapes and arrangements.” The friends wrote down their observations, feeling like real plant detectives. As the sun set over Kandy, Nimali said, “Next time I walk home, I will look at every flower more carefully!”

chapters.chapter_text: On a bright morning, Nethmi stood beside the school garden and looked at the bean plants swaying near the tank. “Sir, how do these plants make their own food?” she asked. Mr. Perera smiled and said that plants are autotrophic, which means they can produce their own food. He tapped a leaf gently and explained that the leaf is the main organ that produces food during photosynthesis. He drew a simple sketch on the board under a mango tree: carbon dioxide enters the leaf through tiny openings called stomata, while water is absorbed by root hairs from the soil and carried to the leaf through xylem. Inside the leaf cells, chlorophyll, the green pigment in chloroplasts, absorbs light energy from sunlight. “These are the important factors for photosynthesis,” he said. “Without them, the plant cannot make food.” The students watched the fish tank, where small bubbles rose from the aquatic plants in the daytime. Mr. Perera explained that oxygen is one of the products of photosynthesis, and that plants also produce glucose. “Later, the glucose made in the leaves is changed into starch, and then it can be changed into sucrose and moved to other parts of the plant,” he said. The children nodded as they imagined the leaf as a tiny food factory. Before the bell rang, Nethmi wrote in her notebook: sunlight + carbon dioxide + water, with chlorophyll, helps plants make food and oxygen. Mr. Perera reminded them that this process is very important for plants and for animals too, because plants support life in many ways. As the wind moved through the garden, the class felt as if the leaves were quietly working together under the sun.

chapters.chapter_text: In his garden in Galle, Nuwan noticed that the plants near the window grew taller than the ones in the shade. His sister explained that plants make their own food using sunlight, in a process called photosynthesis. Inside their green leaves is a substance called chlorophyll, which captures energy from sunlight. The leaves take in carbon dioxide from the air, and the roots draw up water from the soil. Using the sun's energy, the plant combines carbon dioxide and water to make glucose — a sugar it uses as food — and releases oxygen into the air. That oxygen is the very gas we breathe.

chapters.chapter_text: Mr. Perera placed the eye model under the bright lab lamp and asked Amali to find the parts one by one. “The eye is our optical sensory organ,” he said, tapping the model gently. “It sits inside the orbit in the skull and is held by six eye muscles, so it can move up and down, side to side, and even in a circular way. That helps us see a broad area.” Kasun pointed to the white outer layer first. “That is the sclerotic layer,” Mr. Perera nodded. “It is tough and white, and light cannot pass through it. In front, it becomes thin and transparent to form the cornea. Inside it is the choroid, which supplies blood to the eye. Deeper still is the retina, where light-sensitive rod cells and cone cells are found.” Amali then traced the clear parts with her finger. “This watery space is the aqueous humour, and this jelly-like part at the back is the vitreous humour,” she read from the chart. “Good,” said Mr. Perera. “The aqueous humour fills the space between the cornea and the lens, while the vitreous humour helps keep the eye spherical. The iris controls how much light enters, and the pupil is the hole in the centre of the iris. The lens is transparent and biconvex, and the ciliary muscle helps change its curvature when necessary.” At the end of the lesson, Mr. Perera pointed to the back of the model. “The fovea, or yellow spot, is where sharp images are formed,” he said. “The blind spot has no light-sensitive cells, so even if light falls there, no vision is possible. The optic nerve carries the message from the retina to the brain. Next time, we will follow the path of light and learn how the brain understands the image.”

chapters.chapter_text: After school, Nirosha and Kasun sat near the science lab window, watching the golden light fall across the playground. Their teacher, Mrs. Perera, held up a small torch and asked, “How do we see this light?” Nirosha pointed to her eye and said, “With this tiny camera?” Mrs. Perera smiled and began the lesson: the eye has a clear curved front part called the cornea that lets light enter and helps bend it toward the inside. Inside the eye, light passes through the pupil, the dark opening in the centre. The iris, the coloured ring around it, works like a door: it becomes smaller in bright light and larger in dim light to control how much light goes in. Then the lens changes shape to focus the light properly, so nearby and distant objects can look sharp. Kasun blinked and said it was like the eye was adjusting itself all the time. Mrs. Perera drew a simple diagram on the board and explained that the retina at the back of the eye is like a screen made of light-sensitive cells. When light reaches it, messages travel through the optic nerve to the brain. “So the eye only catches the light,” she said, “but the brain understands the picture.” Nirosha nodded, amazed that seeing is actually a teamwork between the eye and the brain. Before they left, the teacher reminded them to care for their eyes by reading in good light and not looking directly at very bright light. Outside, the afternoon sky over Anuradhapura was glowing softly, and Kasun laughed, “Now even a sunset feels like science.” Nirosha smiled, already eager for the next club meeting.

chapters.chapter_text: On Friday afternoon, Amal carried a lime fruit to the science room and smiled. Ms. Perera had asked the club to explore ways of generating electricity, so the children tested a birthday card circuit, a galvanometer, and two thin sheets of copper and zinc. They fixed the copper and zinc into the lime and connected them to the card’s battery places, then watched carefully. The little sound and movement showed them that electricity can be produced from the simple setup, just like in an electric cell. Nethu looked surprised. "So the lime is making electricity?" she asked. Ms. Perera nodded and explained that the galvanometer is a sensitive device used to identify and measure a small current in the laboratory. She also reminded them that people use different methods to generate electricity in different situations. At home, a bicycle dynamo can help, solar cells can power calculators, and dry cells are useful in many small devices. The next day, the class moved to the courtyard for a second activity. They connected a small motor to a galvanometer and then to a tiny bulb, and let running water turn a little turbine made from simple materials. When the turbine spun, the motor acted like a simple dynamo and electricity was generated. Amal remembered that Michael Faraday first discovered that current can be generated by moving a magnet inside a coil of wire. Before the bell rang, Ms. Perera pointed to a map of Sri Lanka and said that large power stations use similar ideas on a bigger scale. Hydropower stations like Kothmale and Victoria use moving water, wind power stations use wind, coal power plants use steam, and fuel power plants use an engine. The club members wrote everything in their notebooks, excited that the same science could light a tiny bulb, run a fan, or power a whole town. The children learn that electricity can be generated in many ways, from a lime fruit to a spinning turbine. Next time, they want to find out which method is best for different places in Sri Lanka.

chapters.chapter_text: After school, Nimal and Ayesha walked to the stream behind their school, where Mr. Perera had brought a small model generator for the science club. “Today,” he said, smiling, “we will see how moving water can help make electricity.” He placed a tiny wheel in the flowing water, and the wheel began to spin. Inside the model was a magnet and a coil of wire, and Mr. Perera explained that this is how a generator works: when a magnet moves near wire, electricity can be produced. Nimal watched closely as the wheel turned faster. “So the water is making the magnet move?” he asked. “Yes,” said Mr. Perera, “and that moving magnet pushes tiny electric charges in the wire. This is called electromagnetic induction.” Ayesha repeated the long word slowly and laughed. Mr. Perera nodded. “In a real power station, water from a dam or river can turn large turbines, and those turbines spin generators to make electricity for homes, schools, and shops.” Later, Mr. Perera showed them a hand-crank torch. When Nimal turned the handle, the bulb lit up. “The same idea,” said the teacher. “We do not create electricity from nothing. We change energy from movement into electrical energy.” Nimal looked toward the stream and imagined the lights in Pussellawa coming on at night because of spinning machines far away. He felt proud that the village’s moving water could do something so useful. On the walk home, Ayesha said, “So electricity starts with energy changing form.” Nimal smiled and answered, “And a generator helps that change happen.” The stream kept rushing beside them, as if it were whispering the lesson again and again.

chapters.chapter_text: Science is all about asking questions and looking carefully at the world around us. A good scientist notices something curious — like why the sky is blue, or why ice melts — and asks 'why?' and 'how?'. They make a testable guess, called a hypothesis, and check it with an experiment. By observing, measuring and recording what happens, we slowly build up reliable knowledge. Even mistakes are useful, because they tell us what does not work and point us toward better answers. Every great discovery began with someone curious enough to test their ideas.

chapters.chapter_text: After school, Amaya and Nilan hurried into the science room, where Mrs. Perera had placed a shiny plane mirror on the desk. “Today,” she said, smiling, “we are learning how images are formed by plane mirrors.” Nilan stood in front of the mirror and waved his right hand, then laughed when the boy in the mirror seemed to wave with his left hand. Mrs. Perera explained that a plane mirror is a flat mirror, and the image it forms is upright, the same size as the object, but laterally inverted, which means left and right appear reversed. Amaya walked closer and then stepped back. “The image moves too!” she said. Mrs. Perera nodded and drew a quick line on the board: the image appears as far behind the mirror as the object is in front of it. She called this the same-distance rule. Nilan measured the space with a ruler and found that when he stood 20 cm from the mirror, his image seemed to be 20 cm behind it. The children were surprised that the mirror did not keep the image inside it, but only made it seem to be there. Next, Mrs. Perera shone a torch at the mirror and asked, “Can we catch the image on a screen?” The children tried, but the image vanished whenever they moved the paper screen behind the mirror. She explained that the image formed by a plane mirror is virtual, which means the light rays only seem to come from behind the mirror and do not actually meet there. “That is why you can see yourself in the mirror, but you cannot place the image on paper,” she said. Amaya nodded slowly, remembering the bathroom mirror at home and the polished steel door of the school lab. Before the bell rang, Mrs. Perera gave them one last challenge: “If you stand straight, the image stands straight too. If you raise your left hand, the image raises its right.” The two friends grinned and practiced mirror poses, turning their lesson into a game. As they left the science room, Nilan said, “So a plane mirror makes an upright, same-size, virtual image that is laterally inverted and appears the same distance behind the mirror.” Mrs. Perera laughed softly. “Excellent,” she said, “next time we will see how mirrors help us in daily life.”

chapters.chapter_text: On a rainy afternoon, Teacher Perera placed a tiny silver phone cover and a pair of smart-looking spectacles on the table. “These are made with nanotechnology,” she said. “Nanotechnology works with matter at the nanoscale, about 1 to 100 nanometres. A nanometre is one billionth of a metre, so this world is unbelievably small.” සඳුනි stared at the phone cover and laughed. “It looks ordinary!” The teacher smiled. “That is the surprise. Tiny structures can make materials very thin, light, strong, and even smart.” She then showed them a picture of memory chips and flexible electronic parts. “With nanotechnology, we can make components that are foldable, stretchable, washable, and even powered by solar energy,” she explained. “It is also used in audio equipment, keyboards with antibacterial covers, and mobile phone covers. In the lab, people even think about tiny machines that can work with microscopic structures.” අරුණ whispered, “So the tiny world can do big jobs?” “Exactly,” said Teacher Perera. “Science can turn small particles into useful tools.” Next, she pointed to another poster showing glasses, filters, and water pipes. “Nanotechnology can help make spectacles and window glass that resist ultraviolet and infrared radiation. Some of these surfaces do not hold water or micro-organisms, so they can clean themselves. Very thin filter membranes can be used in water purification plants, and nanoscale air filters can trap dust. It also helps make durable sports goods, special coatings for machine parts, and cloth that resists dust, dirt, and oil.” Before the bell rang, Teacher Perera became serious. “But every powerful technology must be used carefully,” she said. “Nanotechnology can also create nano pollution if nanoscale particles enter air, water, or soil. So scientists must think about safety, rules, and responsible use.” සඳුනි looked again at the tiny phone cover and felt that the smallest things in science might need the biggest care.

Eric Drexler first published his groundbreaking book "Engines of Creation: The Coming Era of Nanotechnology". Nanotechnology could not really took off until the electron microscopy became popular. chapters.chapter_text: On a rainy afternoon, Ms. Perera placed a small black box on the lab table and smiled. "Today," she said, "we are entering the world of nanotechnology." Nimal frowned. "Nano means tiny, right?" "Yes," Ms. Perera replied. "A nanometer is one-billionth of a meter. That is so small that a human hair is about 80,000 to 100,000 nanometers wide." The three friends stared at each other, amazed that something so tiny could matter so much. Ms. Perera opened the box and showed them a special fabric sample. "At the nanoscale, materials can behave differently," she explained. "The same substance may become stronger, lighter, or more water-resistant." Ayesha touched the cloth and watched a drop of water roll off it like a marble. "So scientists can design tiny particles or coatings to do useful jobs," she said. "Exactly," said Ms. Perera. "These are called nanoparticles—very small particles that can change how a material works." Kasun looked at a packet of medicine on the shelf. Ms. Perera nodded. "Nanotechnology is also used in medicine, solar panels, and water filters. In medicine, it can help carry drugs directly to the right part of the body. In water cleaning, tiny filters can trap harmful particles." Nimal’s eyes widened. "So this is not science fiction at all," he said. "No," smiled Ms. Perera, "it is real science, but it must be used carefully because tiny materials can also have risks if we do not study them properly." As the bell rang, the rain stopped and sunlight touched the wet science garden outside the lab. The friends stepped out talking excitedly about the future. Nimal imagined a school bag with self-cleaning cloth, Ayesha thought about cleaner drinking water for villages, and Kasun wondered what other tiny inventions might help Sri Lanka one day. Ms. Perera locked the lab and said, "Next week, we will see how scientists make nanoparticles and test them safely."
